item.title: Can You Heal from Church Trauma?
item.description:
One of the greatest betrayals is when someone who is supposed to be universally and inherently on your side causes you harm. This type of double-cross has caused great damage throughout history. Look at the way Judas betrayed Christ, or how children of abusive parents grow up with a lion’s share of trauma they must deal with. People still experience this today, even in settings like the church.

Different Types of Trauma

This harmful betrayal is not confined to biblical times or hidden behind closed doors. It can also happen in the larger Christian church body. The church is supposed to be a holy place, filled with Christ-followers. And while this is the ideal and is the case in many healthy congregations, it’s not universally true.

The reality is that the church is a place filled with fallible people, often trying their best. Sometimes they make mistakes. Sometimes they inadvertently hurt each other. And sometimes the church has been infiltrated with sinister people who use the name of Christ to give them authority to do hurtful things.

Abuse in the Church

Some church trauma goes beyond the hurtful to abuse, and in some extreme cases, it’s also criminal. Sexual assault, grooming, spiritual coercion, and the misuse of power by leaders who hide behind their position are all serious violations. These violations can happen even in a church context.

When things like this happen in the church, the damage is tied to a spiritual context. There is something uniquely disorienting about being harmed in a place that is supposed to be a holy refuge. When a leader uses Scripture and the name of God to manipulate and abuse you, it not only affects you emotionally and mentally but can cause significant spiritual damage as well.

Abuse is never justified, even by faith or religious authority. It shouldn’t be tolerated because of tradition or dismissed because of the Christian mandate of forgiveness taken out of context. Abuse done in a church context is explicitly wrong.

If you’ve experienced any type of abuse or exploitation within a church setting, rest assured that it was not your fault, nor was it something you caused. No matter what you did or wore, the responsibility falls entirely on the person who harmed you and anyone who enabled them.

Reporting criminal abuse to the proper authorities is a necessary act of justice that protects both your own safety and the safety of the entire community. Sadly, when abuse happens within the church, leaders sometimes forgo reporting to the authorities.

Less Obvious Harm

Not all church trauma comes from extreme and clearly defined abuse. Sometimes, church trauma is a culmination of a series of repeated negative or careless experiences that slowly push someone out the stained-glass door.

While not abuse, the feeling of being consistently left out of the inner circle can also create a negative association with church. Conversations that stop when you walk into a room and invitations that never come can send the message that you’re not accepted. Favoritism is also damaging to church bodies. When certain people are celebrated, and cliques form within the church, the place of community can start feeling suspiciously similar to a high school cafeteria.

Other times, it is connected to things like serving. While we are called to serve within the church, some churches abuse that power. Even if you were pressured into serving constantly, especially when you see others not contributing, it can cause you to feel used and underappreciated.

If you’ve been a victim of serious trauma at the hands of someone who professed Christianity or was in a Christian authority over you, you know how deeply that betrayal cuts. Even if what caused your church trauma wasn’t illegal or even immoral, it can still leave a scar. Whether your church trauma was truly a result of abuse or just carelessness, the result can be a broken spirit and maybe even a broken relationship with God.

The Aftermath of Abuse

The unfortunate result of abuse in the church is often church trauma. It’s the law of cause and effect in action. If you are harmed by someone who wears the label of Christianity, you are going to associate them and their professed belief with the negative impact it left on you.

Unfortunately, that impact often ripples beyond the initial incident. It can create a deep-seated mistrust toward anything that resembles organized religion. This mistrust can compel people to turn to other non-Christian spiritual beliefs or to develop a disdain for anything associated with Christianity. This change in behavior and belief can carry on throughout a lifetime.

If you’ve been wronged by the church or someone in Christian authority, it might change the way you raise your children. While you might have grown up in the church, your church-related trauma now prevents you from raising your own children within an organized church body.

Sometimes a negative church experience can even impact your relationship with God. It can be difficult to separate what people do in the name of Christ from Christ Himself, especially on an emotional level.

Can you heal?

The short answer is yes, you can overcome church trauma and learn to trust God and His people again. While God can heal and deliver you from the trauma of your past, your healing may require you to invest some time and effort.

Find the truth

To fully heal from church trauma, you need to recognize that the people who represented Christ to you were, in those moments, acting in direct opposition to His nature. Separating the mistakes and actions of a specific person or group from Christ Himself isn’t always easy, especially when those lines were blurred for a long time.

When you do separate the two, you will often find that God is different than how He has been represented. He, too, was wronged by their actions, and while He was innocent, His name and reputation got tarnished in the process.

Get to know Christ

Educate yourself on the nature of Christ. Read the Bible, listen to worship music, and talk with Bible-believing friends about God’s love and nature. By educating yourself, you will discover that Christ brings freedom, love, and grace. You will find that He heals, restores, and loves in a way that is not humanly possible.

Forgive

Depending on the complexity, severity, and duration of your trauma, forgiveness might be difficult. But you don’t have to do it alone. Christ forgave those who murdered Him, and He will help you forgive those who have harmed you, too.

Forgiveness is not justifying their action, but it takes the power away from it and them. When you live in a state of unforgiveness, you are perpetually giving power to the act and the people who have harmed you. But when you release forgiveness, not through your own strength, but in the name of Jesus, you are removing the power your trauma holds over you.

This doesn’t mean that those responsible for your trauma shouldn’t be held accountable for their action. It means that you are making the deliberate decision not to let their actions dictate the rest of your life.

It’s also important to realize that your anger is a righteous response to injustice and that true biblical forgiveness never requires you to remain in a relationship with those who use Scripture as a tool of control or to silence you.

Seek support

Church trauma affects emotional, mental, and relational health, and these are areas that can benefit from professional support.

Working with a licensed Christian therapist can give you the opportunity to fully communicate and understand the experiences that formed your church trauma. It allows you to grieve what was lost and rebuild not only your sense of self, but your relationship with God.

If you’ve been victimized by someone who professed the name of Christ, know that they don’t speak for Him. God loves you unconditionally. He does not approve of abusive behavior, and He wants to heal you. He can help you forgive and to move on to find a body of believers who will help restore true fellowship.

People are fallible and will disappoint you. God is unwavering in His constant love and wants to meet you right where you are. If you have church-related trauma, consider what it might look like to invite God and a professional mental health specialist into the healing process.

Call and schedule an appointment with Joseph. I would be grateful for the opportunity to walk alongside you in this healing journey.

item.title: Night Terrors in Adults: Symptoms, Causes, and Treatment Options
item.description:
Night terrors in adults can be terrifying, especially to those witnessing their loved one during an episode. Nightmares are common and typically happen hours after someone falls asleep. However, night terrors occur during the non-REM sleep, around one to three hours after falling asleep.

Knowing the symptoms and causes of night terrors in adults can help you manage episodes and seek professional help when needed.

Symptoms of Night Terrors in Adults

Symptoms of night terrors in adults can leave one feeling emotionally drained, fatigued, and unstable. The good news is that night terrors tend only to last a few minutes. Once you are aware of the occurrence of night terrors, you can work on managing symptoms.

  • Sudden screaming – Waking up abruptly one to three hours after falling asleep and screaming is a typical sign of a night terror. You may not be aware of your actions, and the screaming may not fully wake you.
  • Thrashing and pushing – People with night terrors may thrash around in bed or push others away. You may wake to find your bed linens and pillows on the floor, or things knocked off the nightstand.
  • Violent behavior – Often, people with night terrors behave violently, as if moving through a nightmare. They may not be awake enough to be aware of others around them.
  • No memory in the morning – Unlike nightmares, you may not remember having a night terror. Others may tell you about it, or you may see the evidence in and around your bed, but have no memory or only a vague memory of the event.

If you feel that you may harm yourself or others during a night terror, seek help immediately.

Causes of Night Terrors in Adults

The causes of night terrors in adults can vary. Factors, including environmental factors, may play a role. A counselor can help you delve into the underlying cause of your sleep disruption and assist you in managing behaviors.

  • Trauma and PTSD – Unresolved trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) can trigger night terrors. Many people find that therapy helps them through trauma disorders.
  • Anxiety – Anxiety and chronic stress can work as underlying factors while you try to rest and sleep. Your subconscious can wake you as your mind tries to process perceived danger.
  • Extreme Stress – Extreme stress can result in chronic inflammation in the body, which can disrupt sleep. The body’s stress response releases adrenaline and cortisol in the body. In a constant state, the body stays in fight-or-flight mode.
  • Depression – Depression can increase your risk of sleep deprivation, poor sleep quality, and disruptions. Studies show that nightmares may lead to a higher risk of suicidal thoughts or self-harm. The studies did not elaborate whether the subjects suffered from only nightmares or if night terrors were grouped into the category.
  • Alcohol or Drug Abuse – Alcohol and substance abuse raise your risk of developing night terrors.
  • Genetics and Family History – Genetics and family history play a role in your risk of experiencing night terrors. Also, age is a crucial factor. Night terrors may re-emerge if the person suffered from them as a child and is extremely stressed or is the victim of trauma.

A counselor can help you determine the factors behind your night terrors and create a mental health plan to assist you in overcoming them.

Treatment for Night Terrors

Treatments for night terrors can include lifestyle alternatives to lower stress and anxiety, combined with counseling to move past obstacles that may be hindering your progress. As with anything of value, results may not be instantaneous. However, over time, you should have fewer incidences of night terrors and be better equipped to handle them.

  • Counseling – Talk therapy and Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) may help get to the root of the night terrors and help in changing thoughts and behaviors.
  • Scheduled Wakeup Times – To offset the beginning of a night terror, try scheduling a wake-up time to disrupt the pattern. This is a temporary solution, as you are disrupting sleep. However, because night terrors typically occur within the first three hours of sleep, you have a much better chance of breaking the pattern. Consult with a sleep specialist and your counselor about a long-term solution.
  • Stress Management – Most night terrors are brought on by extreme or chronic stress. Learning stress-management and relaxation techniques and adopting healthy lifestyle habits could help reduce the occurrence of night terrors.

Your counselor may have more suggestions for lifestyle tweaks that could reduce the frequency of night terrors.

Christian Counseling Can Help with Night Terrors in Adults

Are night terrors making it difficult to rest? Are you worried about hurting yourself or others during an episode? Contact our office today to speak with a Christian counselor about treatment options, including Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT). Night terrors in adults can be addressed with lifestyle alternatives and Christian counseling treatments. Contact us today to get started.

item.title: Understanding and Treating Food Addiction as an Addictive Behavior
item.description:
Food addiction is a behavior that can interfere with your mental and physical health, lower self-esteem and confidence, and leave you with feelings of guilt and shame.

What is Addictive Behavior?

Addictive behavior is a behavior that provides temporary pleasure and reinforces the action, creating pathways in the brain that make it difficult to stop engaging in. There are various types of addictive behavior. You can be addicted to substances, work, shopping, gambling, sex, gaming, social media, alcohol, and food.

How to Move Past Addictive Behavior

When it comes to addictive behavior with food, managing actions can feel challenging. You cannot avoid food, unlike other substances or behaviors, such as shopping or social media. Moving past addictive behavior means learning how to identify and reframe negative thoughts and behaviors. A counselor can teach you Cognitive Behavioral Therapy techniques that will help you shift your thoughts and behaviors.

The following are several ways to move past food addiction.

Journal meals and snacks Food addiction can lead you to mindlessly eat when you are not physically hungry and eat more than is necessary. By journaling your meals and snacks, along with the emotions you experience before, during, and after each meal, you can collect data on your habits. You will be able to identify triggers, thoughts, feelings, and consumption that you can share with your counselor, if needed.

Check in with your hunger levels Food addiction is an urge to eat when not hungry. This behavior is attached to a trigger. Check in with your hunger levels before giving in to the impulse. Is your stomach growling, or does it feel empty?

Take it one meal at a time Stop telling yourself that you will be perfect as you overcome food addiction. Give yourself grace for reaching for food when not hungry as you practice techniques to break free. Take it one meal at a time. Don’t think about the last meal or the next, and instead, stay in the present moment. You can say no when you are not hungry and busy your hands doing something else. Don’t allow distractions to derail you.

Remove problem foods for now If there are specific foods in your pantry or refrigerator that make it difficult for you to walk away, consider removing them temporarily until you are better practiced with coping mechanisms. You can add them back once you feel confident. Or, allow yourself to only consume them while hungry during a meal in public, as many people struggling with food addiction eat in secret.

Don’t deprive yourself of your favorite treats, as that can lead to bingeing. Instead, treat yourself to a moderate amount. For example, if the food you have impulse problems with is ice cream (or any high-sugar, high-fat, or high-sodium food), schedule a time when you can have one serving.

Perhaps allow yourself to have a cone once a week from a favorite ice cream place. Wait until you are physically hungry before eating the ice cream cone. By treating yourself outside of the environment where you might emotionally eat, such as at home, you break the addictive behavior cycle and are less likely to eat mindlessly.

Counseling Help for Addictive Behavior

If the addictive behavior of food addiction and emotional eating leaves you feeling out of control, contact our office today to schedule a session with a Christian counselor. A representative will match you with a counselor specializing in addictive behavior and disordered eating. Call us today to get started.

item.title: Constantly Frustrated? Scriptures on Forgiveness To Help Cope With Daily Pressures
item.description:
Isn’t it strange how easily frustration can sneak into our lives? Life doesn’t always give you space to breathe. Plans fall apart, or someone says the wrong thing, and you feel that familiar tension rise. You try to move on, but it lingers.

Pressure starts to feel like part of your routine, something you’ve learned to live with. You promise yourself you’ll respond better next time, but frustration keeps winning. It’s not that you don’t want peace; you just don’t know how to hold onto it.

Living in that constant state of irritation drains your peace and makes it harder to connect with others or even hear yourself think.

Remember, there are powerful scriptures on forgiveness that can speak directly to the heart. The Bible doesn’t just tell us to “let it go.” It reminds us that forgiveness is a daily practice that reshapes how you respond to pressure, not just how you handle hurt.

Why Frustration Keeps You Caught in the Same Cycle

Frustration normally doesn’t just pop up out of nowhere. It builds from small disappointments that pile up until you start reacting instead of reflecting. You tell yourself you’re fine, but your body and mind know otherwise. Then the tension shows up in your tone, your thoughts, and even your sleep.

When frustration becomes your default response, it’s easy to lose sight of grace. You start expecting others to change before you can feel better. Forgiveness, as taught in Scripture, can flip that pattern. It invites you to release what’s weighing you down, even when the situation hasn’t changed.

True forgiveness means choosing peace over bitterness. It’s a quiet decision that says, “I won’t let this moment define my spirit.”

Which Scriptures on Forgiveness Teach About Pressure

Forgiveness in Scripture isn’t just about relationships; it’s also about how you handle life’s daily stress. When Jesus spoke of forgiving “seventy times seven,” He wasn’t merely setting a number; He was describing a lifestyle.

It’s only that kind of forgiveness that can help you respond to pressure with patience instead of resentment. We’ve made a list of verses that may not be the ones people quote most often, but they speak powerfully to the kind of frustration that builds up in ordinary life.

Bear with each other and forgive one another if any of you has a grievance against someone. Forgive as the Lord forgave you. – Colossians 3:13, NIV

This verse reminds you that forgiveness is a shared responsibility, not a one-time act. When someone’s words sting or their habits wear you down, this Scripture reminds you to think before reacting.

Practical takeaway: When you feel pressure rising, ask yourself, Am I expecting perfection from someone who is only human, just like me?

A person’s discretion makes him slow to anger, and it is his glory to overlook a transgression. – Proverbs 19:11, NASB

This verse doesn’t tell you to ignore pain; it teaches discernment. Overlooking an offense means deciding which battles are worth your peace. Wisdom helps you see that not every irritation deserves your energy.

Practical takeaway: When frustration hits, take a mental step back and ask, Will this matter tomorrow? If not, let it pass. That’s how forgiveness becomes a quiet strength instead of a forced reaction.

Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander be put away from you, along with all malice. Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you. – Ephesians 4:31-32, ESV

This verse speaks directly to emotional buildup. Forgiveness here is described as an act of compassion, not convenience. It’s a way to clear emotional clutter so you can think and respond clearly.

Practical takeaway: When you feel yourself replaying an argument or holding onto resentment, stop and pray for compassion instead of control. Forgiveness starts where empathy begins.

Refrain from anger and turn from wrath; do not fret – it leads only to evil. – Psalm 37:8, NIV

This verse speaks of the spiral of irritation that comes with daily stress. “Do not fret” isn’t just advice; it’s a reminder that constant frustration can distort your peace.

Practical takeaway: When you feel tension building, remind yourself that fretting doesn’t fix anything.

And whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father also who is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses. – Mark 11:25, ESV

This verse connects forgiveness to prayer, showing that emotional release and spiritual clarity go hand in hand. It’s not about earning God’s favor; it’s about clearing space in your heart so that your prayers aren’t weighed down by resentment.

Practical takeaway: Before you pray about stress or frustration, take a moment to forgive someone or something, even silently.

There will be days when forgiveness feels impossible, when the hurt is too fresh or the frustration too deep. That’s when it helps to talk to someone who understands both faith and emotional healing.

If frustration has been controlling your days, it’s time to take a step toward peace. You don’t have to keep managing pressure alone. Call the numbers on the screen and start learning how forgiveness can help you breathe again, think clearly, and live with a lighter heart.

item.title: Stay Local: Ways to Improve Your Mental Health Without Going Far
item.description:
Improving our mental health is often about the small choices we make every day. Making choices to eat more fruits and vegetables, drink more water, and get enough sleep are all essential ways to boost your mental and physical health.

We can also enhance our mental health through various activities within our communities. In this article, we will suggest four places/people to visit as a way to improve your mental health.

Visit the Local Library

Libraries are cornerstones of community. Not only do you have access to every genre of literature available, but there are often clubs and gatherings that meet in libraries. Librarians can share information about community events, classes, and other ways of social engagement.

Many libraries offer lending programs that extend beyond books. Board games, tools to try out new hobbies, and even apps that give you access without taking dollars from your bank account. Using the library to enhance your mental health is beneficial from multiple angles. Whether it’s escaping into fiction, learning something about the world, or gathering with community, the options for improving your mental health are only limited by your choices.

Visit State and City Parks

Being outdoors is known to boost your mental health. The physical activity, the fresh air, and being surrounded by plant and creature life all provide you with small doses of serotonin, the hormone that increases happiness. State parks are often inexpensive and easy ways to learn about the flora and fauna that are native to your area. City parks typically offer a range of amenities, including sports complexes, playgrounds, and well-maintained walking paths.

When being outdoors is not an option due to weather, other commitments, or location, there are still ways to enjoy life. Try setting a soothing nature background on your television. Check out the livestream of your favorite zoo. Visit an indoor garden or keep a plant in your home. Even these small ways of engaging with nature can boost your mental health.

Visit With Your Friends

One of the hallmarks of anxiety, depression, burnout, etc., is a change in socializing. Getting together with friends can improve mental health, even if you don’t confide in them. Gathering to play, talk, or eat together can go a long way to improving mental health. Being in person will always be the best, but a long phone conversation when getting together is impossible can also boost your mental health.

If inviting people to your home is stressful, plan to meet elsewhere. Some people ask others to their houses to motivate them to clean. Some friends might be great for a game at one of the local parks, while others could be part of a book club. Having an in-person connection does not need to be about depth and spilling your guts. Building relationships around fun is often the road to a deeper connection when things get tough.

Visit with a Therapist to Improve Your Mental Health

Talk therapy plays a significant role in improving mental health. Even if you are not going through a tough season, therapists can provide valuable insights into your life and areas for growth. If your therapist has been through tough times with you, they can celebrate the wins just as well. If you are looking for talk therapy, you can call our offices today, and we will arrange an appointment for you.

Photos:
“Asian beautiful woman”, Courtesy of Getty Images, Unsplash.com, Unsplash+ License;

The post Stay Local: Ways to Improve Your Mental Health Without Going Far appeared first on Longview Christian Counseling.

item.title: When to Seek PTSD Help So You Can Feel Better
item.description:
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is a mental condition affecting roughly 13 million people in the United States annually. The trauma disorder interferes with daily activities if left untreated, as well as disrupts relationships and responsibilities.

Knowing when to seek help can enable you to work with a counselor to build a customized plan for managing symptoms of PTSD.

Signs to Seek PTSD Help

The symptoms of PTSD can cause mental distress and physical issues. Unfortunately, many people may be unaware that the anxiety they feel is Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder. People seek PTSD help after the following:

  • Involved in a violent event, such as war
  • Witnessing a traumatic event
  • Being abandoned, neglected, or abused
  • Being under great pressure for a period of time, such as caregiving for a terminal loved one

Anyone can develop PTSD, not just war veterans, although that is the demographic most associated with PTSD. For example, a woman caring for her terminal mother may develop PTSD symptoms due to chronic stress and worry. A teenage boy may show symptoms if he was neglected or abused during early childhood.

Christian counseling is effective for managing PTSD symptoms. Your counselor will combine evidence-based techniques with faith-based principles to address you as a whole person: physically, mentally, and spiritually.

The following are signs that you may need PTSD help.

Persistent Reactions

If you experience persistent reactions to noise or other triggers, you could be showing a sign of PTSD. People who have experienced trauma often physically react to triggers. For example, a war veteran may duck when they hear a loud bang. A woman may suffer a panic attack during a storm because she lived through a natural disaster, such as a tornado.

Startling, ducking, and high anxiety due to a trigger that occurs for more than four weeks indicate that a mental health professional should see you. Counseling is not lifelong. You learn the skills you need to manage and overcome PTSD symptoms spread out over several sessions.

Interference with Daily Life

Memories and traumatic behavior (like the startle response or panic attacks) can interfere with your daily activities. You may find yourself withdrawing from others or preferring to work from home. You may feel embarrassment, guilt, or shame in your reactions.

Yet, isolation is never the answer. Learning to overcome panic attacks, anxiety, depression, and intrusive memories can bolster your self-esteem and confidence. You are a work in progress, and God never intended for you to walk through this alone. Counseling and support can help you get back to what is important to you.

Intrusive Thoughts

Intrusive thoughts and memories are strong, vivid images and urges. If you suffer from PTSD, you may have experienced these. Intrusive thoughts can be scary and seem to come out of nowhere. They can make you want to give in and do things you wouldn’t normally do. Sometimes, these thoughts can feel true. False beliefs arise from intrusive thoughts.

Intrusive memories can appear as realistic flashbacks. Some people have experienced such vivid flashbacks that the line between reality and memory blurs. It can take several minutes to return to reality, though the physical effects (rapid heart rate, shallow breathing, high blood pressure) can persist for hours.

Emotional Symptoms

Intense emotions can plague someone dealing with PTSD. Shame, guilt, sadness, and anger can stem from the event or chronic situation that has led to the trauma disorder. You may feel empty and numb, detached from others around you, and unable to connect with friends and family.

Thought distortions about yourself or others can cause riffs where none exist. Paranoia can also contribute to feelings of loneliness. The emotional upheaval can lead to other anxiety and depressive disorders if left untreated.

Physical Symptoms

The mind is a powerful thing. Anxiety and depression can fuel changes in brain chemistry and the nervous system. Physical symptoms can develop, including:

  • Rapid or irregular heart rate
  • High blood pressure
  • Appetite changes
  • Rapid weight gain or loss
  • Poor sleep quality
  • Forgetfulness or brain fog
  • Unexplainable pain
  • Digestive issues
  • Headaches
  • Skin rashes or itchiness

Physical and emotional symptoms can combine to leave you feeling unworthy and isolated from the world. If you or someone you love is having thoughts of harming themselves or others, or struggles with suicidal thoughts, seek help immediately.

Counseling for PTSD

If you are seeking PTSD help, we can assist you in your search. Contact us today to speak to a representative who will connect you to a Christian counselor specializing in trauma disorders. PTSD help is only a call or click away.

“Man sitting”, Courtesy of Kelly Sikkema, Unsplash.com, CC0 License

item.title: Overcoming Negative Thoughts from a Christian Counseling Perspective
item.description:
Negative thoughts and beliefs can create a loop, influencing your emotions and perceptions. Have you ever had a fleeting thought that changed how you felt? Perhaps you were happy, and a sudden thought occurred to you, and you felt down, sad, or even worthless.

Negative thoughts trigger our emotions and influence our actions in response. But you can overcome negative thoughts with a few psychological techniques.

Tips for Overcoming Negative Thoughts

Negative thoughts can sound true until you challenge them. Learning how to identify and “catch” your thoughts, manage them, and seek help when needed can shift your perspective and emotions.

The following are tips for overcoming negative thoughts. Try each one. They may feel uncomfortable at first, but as you continue to become more aware of the words you say to yourself, you will identify a pattern. A counselor can help you break the cycle.

“Catch” Your Thoughts

As a Holy Spirit-filled Christian, you have the divine weapons to “demolish arguments and every pretension that sets itself up against the knowledge of God, and we take captive every thought to make it obedient to Christ.” (2 Corinthians 10:6, NIV)

It is time to “catch” your own thoughts, taking them captive. Start paying close attention to the words you say aloud, the thoughts driving these words, and your actions. Take note of your emotions. If you notice you suddenly feel depressed or on edge, ask yourself what you were thinking about. Identify the negative thoughts that started the spiral.

Challenge Negative Thoughts

Not everything you think is true. Negative thoughts can seem true, and are often the result of black-and-white thinking (all-or-nothing), catastrophizing (this always happens), or mind-reading (you just know what someone else is thinking or saying).

Challenge these thoughts with the truth. Recognize the mind’s strategy. Ask yourself if what you think is really true.

Reframe Negative Thoughts

Once you have identified the negative thoughts and the strategy, reframe them around the truth. For example, you have no way of knowing what someone is thinking. Often, situations are not clear-cut, so all-or-nothing thinking will not get you anywhere. Consider leaving specific phrases out of your vocabulary for a while, such as saying, “This always happens to me!” or “I bet that happens.”

Work on reframing negative thoughts. Instead of thinking, “I bet she thought I was ignorant,” reframe the thought with, “I have no idea what she was thinking, but I did well, and I’m proud of myself.”

Journal Your Thoughts and Emotions to Reveal Patterns

Identifying and reframing negative thoughts might be easier if you consider journaling your thoughts and emotions to reveal thought and behavioral patterns. When you notice a negative thought, record it in your journal. Ask yourself if it is true and what thought strategy is behind it. Next, write out a reframing statement to counter the negative thought.

A counselor can help you identify patterns and create positive statements to say to yourself when the negative thoughts repeat.

When Negative Thoughts Seem Insurmountable

Sometimes, negative thoughts can seem insurmountable. They can convince us of lies and skew our perception of the truth. This misperception can lead to anxiety, depression, mood disorders, and other mental health conditions.

Contact our office today to schedule a session with a Christian counselor. The counselors in our network offer virtual and in-person sessions, and would love to help you overcome negative thoughts by arming you with the strategies to manage them for good. Speak to a representative today.

item.title: Adverse Childhood Experiences and the Hidden Cost of Growing Up in a Conflict-Free Home
item.description:
It may seem strange to say that quiet households aren’t necessarily healthy. Homes where there are no arguments between the parents, no slamming doors, and no visible discord are often depicted as the perfect home environment. But there are times that this perfect environment feels off. There’s an unnamed uneasiness, lingering in the shadows. Adverse childhood experiences aren’t just a product of loud and volatile environments.

These experiences often have roots embedded in homes where there was no conflict. In these homes, the silence itself has become the message. It’s important to pay attention to this as Scripture is clear about how to raise children:

“Train up a child in the way he should go, even when he is old he will not depart from it.” Proverbs 22:6, NASB 1995

Adverse Childhood Experiences in the Spaces Between the Words

Society commonly associates adverse childhood experiences with obvious harm such as abuse, neglect, or a household shaped by addiction or violence. But the definition reaches far beyond those familiar categories.

Other areas connected to adverse childhood experiences are emotional unavailability, chronically unresolved dynamics, or emotional environments that children absorb before they have a language to describe them. When conflict is permanently suppressed within a home, a different set of messages is sent.

Children are more perceptive than parents give them credit for. They notice when there is a proverbial elephant in the room that no one is talking about. The weight of unspoken disagreements and a cool distance between their parents are things that children can pick up on, even though no words have been spoken. What they see, and what they don’t see, is quietly shaping the way they understand the dynamics of relationships and how they should work.

When conflict is avoided, children often grow up believing that any form of disagreement is unsafe. This leaves them navigating adulthood without knowing how to have hard conversations in a way that doesn’t end in shutting down or walking away. This results in the lesson that conflict must be avoided at all costs rather than worked through. This is a lesson that most people do not recognize until adulthood.

How Adverse Childhood Experiences Shape Emotional Development

The emotional map that children use to navigate their feelings, relationships, and sense of self stems from the emotional landscape they grow up in. Christian counselors emphasize that individuals who present with anxiety, emotional avoidance, or difficulty sustaining a close relationship can trace those patterns back to early home environments.

These environments were not always chaotic, but they did lack emotional honesty. A conflict-free home doesn’t mean it is automatically healthy. The difference between these two types of homes matters in how a child’s emotional development happens.

Adults who were raised in households where healthy disagreement was never modeled often develop a heightened sensitivity to perceived social threats. These adults can read the room and learn to manage the emotions of those around them, quietly disappearing into whatever version of themselves fits the situation.

This leads to an internal fracture that masks a persistent, ongoing dilemma of not knowing whether their own feelings are acceptable. These adults spend many years managing others instead of realizing they have never learned to manage themselves. Emotional suppression in the home can give way to lasting difficulties in emotional regulation, self-worth, and relational intimacy. The soul will carry what the mind cannot yet fully process.

Faith, Healing, and the Permission to Feel

Scripture gives us a profound gift centered on the permission to feel emotions. The book of Psalms is a testament that God does not require positive feelings all the time. Grief, frustration, lament, and longing are woven throughout the biblical narrative from Genesis to Revelation. Adults who grapple with the residue of a childhood spent trying to understand emotional silence can understand the transformation of this biblical narrative.

God created us and does not demand that we hide our feelings; he invites them. He welcomes our open, honest feelings so He can comfort us and work in us.

Christian counselors understand that the healing process from early relational wounds is not a straight line. The adult will be required to learn how to identify emotions that were never given names or sit with discomfort that was once suppressed. They will need to understand how to rebuild a sense of what a safe connection feels and looks like.

These things can be found when faith serves as a foundation. This leads to confidence that God is present in the slow, hard process of becoming whole. This principle is the basis for genuine and lasting change.

The spiritual aspect of this process is significant in helping adults identify how they have internalized a distorted image of God as a result of growing up in conflict-avoidant homes. It removes the lens that says God is emotionally unavailable and requires composed compliance instead of a relationship. Scripture dismantles this image and offers one that says God draws near in the places we keep most guarded.

“Do not fear, for I am with you; Do not be afraid, for I am your God. I will strengthen you, I will also help you, I will also uphold you with My righteous right hand.” – Isaiah 41:10, NASB

Support for What You Could Not Name

One of the most complex dynamics adults experience is difficulty identifying what is wrong. They have no recollection of a dramatic event or of any identifiable wound. But they know that they have lingering effects in relationships and emotional availability.

They noticed that their sense of self was affected, and Christian counselors can provide the essential help needed to understand what happened. The result will be healing that is possible and worth pursuing.

When adults are willing to seek support, they are choosing to take an honest look at what they absorbed in childhood. It doesn’t mean they need to assign blame, but rather to bring the unnamed experiences into the light for addressing.

This will illuminate a connection between early emotional environments and their current relational patterns, allowing them to relax. They find they no longer need to maintain an impossible balancing act and can move forward with the healing that comes from naming the struggle.

Faith is a reminder that we are not required to carry these struggles alone. We were not designed to carry the burdens alone. Through community and honest conversations, we find that it is not weakness but rather reinforcement that will create a flourishing lifestyle based on the life that Scripture points to. We are reminded of God’s faithfulness to care for us in Psalm 147: “He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.” (Psalm 147:3, NASB)

Moving Toward Wholeness

It may not look like an issue that causes a struggle, but homes without healthy conflict create a specific kind of loss. It is a loss that goes unnamed and unknown for years. The face of a quiet adverse childhood experience is not easy to recognize, yet it is important to address. It is not an easy thing to name what happened in relation to adverse childhood experiences, but it is where everything shifts.

We don’t surprise God with our baggage. There is no distance from the layers of work that come with healing from what we absorbed before we could speak the words. Our journey toward wholeness doesn’t require having everything figured out. It only asks that we be willing to start and trust that we are not on the road alone. God is faithful to work things out for His good.

“And we know that God causes all things to work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called according to His purpose.” – Romans 8:28, NASB

Can you identify with any of this information? If so, please do not hesitate to contact the office and speak with the reception team. They can get you set up with an appointment to meet with the right counselor and start your journey to heal the wounds that have gone unnamed.

item.title: Finding Healing for the Wounds of Moral Trauma
item.description:
When you think of the word ‘trauma,’ what most likely comes to mind is something that’s been done to you or another person. That trauma could come from experiences such as acts of violence or even being caught up in a natural disaster.

There are other forms and sources of trauma, and they include the burden on your soul that results from spiritual and psychological distress. This moral trauma can strike at the heart of who you are, affecting your well-being.

Deep pain doesn’t just result from physical injury. At times, some of the deepest pains we carry are inflicted through other means. When your conscience and moral compass are violated, for instance, leaving you feeling disoriented, you may wonder whether you can be made whole again and if you can make your world make sense once more. Moral trauma, or moral injury, can be resolved, and you can find healing and transformation.

The Anatomy of Moral Trauma

Distress doesn’t only come from situations where you feel at risk or physically threatened. We are physical and spiritual beings. We can experience things that burden our souls and consciences, and that is where moral trauma resides.

Moral trauma, which is also sometimes referred to as moral injury, is the spiritual and psychological distress that arises when a person feels that they’ve violated their own moral or ethical beliefs.

Violation of your own beliefs strikes at the heart of who you are as a person; it can leave you feeling sullied, broken, confused, and in need of healing. When you feel betrayed by your own actions or inaction, or when others’ actions compromise you deeply, it’s a huge blow that strikes at who you are as a person. Often, the way toward healing will require new self-discovery and rebuilding what was lost.

Moral trauma differs somewhat from many forms of physical or emotional trauma. These often stem from a single life-threatening experience or event, while moral trauma can occur in those and other circumstances. When a person violates their own deeply held ethical or moral beliefs, or when they are put in a situation where they are powerless to stop such a violation, that can result in the distress that informs moral trauma.

When you’re traumatized by an assault, a natural disaster, or an accident, the typical result is that your fear response is triggered and becomes overstimulated. You may have nightmares, become hypervigilant, or engage in avoidance behaviors where you steer clear of the places, people, or situations that remind you of the incident. Moral trauma centers more on the loss of moral integrity, and it is rooted in shame, guilt, and the sense of spiritual disconnection one feels.

How and When Moral Trauma Occurs

In what sort of circumstances does moral trauma occur? The weight of moral trauma is rooted in what happened and what that means for one’s sense of right and wrong. The rupture of your personal and spiritual identity is a different sort of animal than the fear that gets unleashed by other forms of trauma and the reality of post-traumatic stress.

Moral trauma can occur in extraordinary situations where ethical dilemmas and human suffering intertwine, but it can also occur in everyday circumstances, too. Some of the contexts in which moral trauma may occur include situations where individuals may witness or participate in actions that conflict deeply with their moral compass, such as for those in law enforcement or the military.

This trauma may also result for individuals in healthcare or for first responders, where they make choices in life-or-death situations that feel ethically complicated or impossible to resolve. If you value life, making hard choices involving the lives of others can affect you deeply, and possibly lead to moral trauma.

In situations when you’re interacting or dealing with someone in a position of moral or spiritual authority, violations of trust, such as abuse or betrayal by such individuals, can be disorienting and traumatizing. It’s hard to reconcile your conception of the individual and their behavior, leading to a moment of crisis.

Lastly, moral trauma can also happen in everyday situations, such as moral compromise. This includes feeling complicit in wrongdoing by being silent or not doing anything about it. It can look like going along with a lie your boss tells at work or yielding to a bully by not intervening and protecting those who can’t protect themselves.

In these and other instances, what happens is an experience of deep inner turmoil that’s hard to reconcile. Witnessing or participating in something that violates your conscience or moral code can result in moral trauma, particularly if you don’t know how to process it or don’t have the support you need to work through it.

How Moral Trauma Can Affect You

While most other forms of trauma affect your fear response, moral trauma affects your spiritual well-being primarily, as well as impacts every other facet of your well-being. Spiritually and emotionally, moral trauma can leave you feeling far from the Lord, questioning your faith, and perhaps even being afraid of the Lord’s lack of favor or judgment. It’s a deeply upsetting and unsettling place to be.

Additionally, moral trauma can impact you by loading you with persistent guilt, anger, shame, and self-condemnation. As you remember what happened and try to make sense of it, you may be overwhelmed by these emotions and the feeling of failure.

Physically, moral trauma can result in disturbed sleep, ailments that are closely related to stress, like high blood pressure or stomach ulcers, and chronic fatigue. Mentally, you may experience difficulty concentrating on your tasks, as well as a sense of moral disorientation. The experience scrambles your sense of right and wrong as well as your place in the universe. You may also experience intrusive memories or unwanted flashbacks of the experience.

Last but not least, moral trauma also affects you relationally. As you try to make sense of things, you might find yourself withdrawing from loved ones, struggling to receive forgiveness or love from others, and you might also distrust others and yourself as well. At a time when you need others most, moral trauma can draw you toward isolation, which makes things more difficult. However – thank the Lord – there are pathways to healing from moral trauma.

Finding Healing for the Wounds of Moral Trauma

Even when you feel like you’ve let yourself, the Lord, and others down, life still has meaning, and it can be full of joy once again. We are all broken, and we act inconsistently and out of alignment with our deepest beliefs. The path of discipleship and following Jesus is about learning and growing to become the people we already are, by grace, in Him. In Christ, our brokenness and broken stories can be redeemed.

It’s hard to shake the shadow of moral compromise and the weight of trauma that it can load upon our shoulders. It is possible to surrender guilt and shame, embracing forgiveness and the wholeness that Jesus brings (John 10:10). Whatever you’ve experienced or done doesn’t have to control or shape the rest of your life. Some life-giving steps you can take include:

Acknowledgment and Confession Light is an amazing disinfectant, and that applies to our moral wrongdoings as well. Bring the hurt, inconsistency, guilt, and failure into the open. Psalm 51 is an amazingly honest reflection on moral failings that can result in moral trauma, and it can set the pattern for your own reflections, acknowledgment, and confession before the Lord.

Reframe Things The disorientation you experience from moral trauma can be counteracted by grounding yourself again in the truths of God’s word. There, you encounter truth bound up with grace, mercy, and forgiveness, which can help you reframe what you experienced. Consider and reflect on John 8:1-11; John 21:15-19; 1 Timothy 1:15-17; and Romans 8.

Acts of Service Guilt can be transformed into growth and purpose when you engage in acts of service or seek reconciliation where appropriate. It’s not so much that you’re making up for anything, because in Christ our debt is paid in full (Colossians 2:6-15), but it’s leaning into and living according to your purpose in Him.

Seek a Safe Community and Counsel Our lives aren’t meant to be lived in isolation, even in those moments when we are struggling to endure our own company. Share your story with others like a trusted and wise friend, a spiritual advisor, or a professional Christian counselor. This is an important step in dismantling the isolation that moral trauma often creates.

You can find help from a professional Christian counselor who uses trauma-informed therapy and faith-based resources to help you find healing and hope. Reach out today to connect with someone who can help you overcome the wounds of moral trauma.

item.title: Finding Freedom from Fear: A Christian Counselor’s Personal Story
item.description:
Fear is an essential survival mechanism that elicits both physical and emotional reactions. When you sense a threat, fear is protective. However, fear can be overwhelming if it is out of balance and out of proportion to the risks. Maintaining psychological balance requires an understanding of the nature of fear and practical coping strategies.

For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power and of love and of a sound mind – 2 Tim. 1:7, NKJV

My Journey Into Fear

Personally, I spent years living in fear. As a child, I was afraid of the dark. Fear followed me into adulthood, marriage, moving to a bigger city, then motherhood, and my home. Although I loved God and trusted Him, I couldn’t seem to silence the constant “what ifs” that stole my peace.

One thing that magnified my fears was the news. As long as I can remember, I’ve noticed a trend on the news and then eventually on social media: fear.

There is always something on the news or happening in the world that could make us fearful: wars, pandemics, health issues, job insecurity, the health and welfare of our children, other anxieties and phobias, etc. I got sucked into the news after 9/11. So, in 2020, after the news of the pandemic, I had to stop watching or reading the news.

I had faith; I believed in God, and deep down I knew He would protect us. But I couldn’t shake that grip that fear had on me. I would pray over our house, walk around and pray over our property, etc., but nothing seemed to help the fear subside.

I had trouble sleeping because of my fears of someone breaking into our home. I bought a little picture of an angel guarding a child’s bed and every night began to recite the passage that was printed on it: Psalm 4:8, “In peace I will lie down and sleep, for you alone, LORD, make me dwell in safety.”

I had been reading The Power of a Praying Parent by Stormie Omartian and read the chapter on fear, not just for my daughter, but for me. It was pretty humbling. I tried to read other books on fear, but they all dealt with things such as stage fright, asking for a raise, etc. Those are still real and debilitating fears, but I felt like I was the only person who was fearing for my life.

A Prisoner of Fear

Looking back, I realize I was truly a prisoner to my own mind and emotions. On top of the fear, I was dealing with so many other “issues.” God began to slowly peel away at those issues one by one, but it truly took faith to overcome the fear.

Neil T. Anderson (2017) reminds us, “Fear is a God-given natural response when our physical or psychological safety is threatened. Fear always has an object, that is something or someone, and that object must be both present and potent, that is perceived to have some power over us. It ceases to be a fear object when only one of those attributes is eliminated” (p. 28).

He goes on to explain, The fear of people, death, and Satan is the root of almost all fears. Death is still present since it is a real possibility, but once we believe in Jesus and accept Him as our Lord and Savior, it is no longer powerful (1 Cor. 15:54-55).

Although fear is a normal human reaction, sometimes anxiety and fear become more than occasional worry. I realize that, for some individuals, anxiety can involve biological, psychological, and environmental factors that require additional support. But for now, I am talking mostly about fear that is out of balance and has no real threat.

In counseling, we often talk about how our thoughts influence our emotions and behaviors. Fear thrives on repeated messages of danger, while faith grows when we intentionally focus on truth. Another perspective that helped me was understanding fear as misplaced faith – placing belief in what might go wrong rather than in God’s promises.

Looking back, I can see how fear grew stronger when I repeatedly focused on threatening information. The more I watched the news and imagined worst-case scenarios, the more my mind became trained to anticipate danger.

The Nature of Fear

As a counselor, I have seen how anxiety can affect even the strongest believers. Experiencing anxiety does not mean someone lacks faith, nor does seeking counseling, medical care, or medication indicate spiritual weakness.

God often works through the wisdom, support, and resources He provides through others. Just as we seek treatment for physical illnesses, there are times when receiving professional support for our mental and emotional well-being is an important part of healing.

One resource God used during my journey was a small booklet called Freedom From Fear. While I don’t believe one book is the answer for everyone, God used its biblical perspective to help me recognize how fear had shaped my thinking. For some reason, reading it made that little lightbulb in my brain turn on. I had that “Aha” moment.

“There are two spiritual laws at work in the world today: the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus and the law of sin and death. The force of faith comes from life. The force of fear comes from death” (back cover). In the booklet, the law of reciprocals (“corresponding, but reversed or inverted” principles) is discussed in Romans 8:2: “For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has made me free from the law of sin and death.”

Understanding that fear is just faith perverted (by Satan) opened my eyes. Satan is “limited to the forces of the world.” He cannot create or come up with new ideas. He just perverts the spiritual laws that are already in place. “Sin was not a new law. It was righteousness perverted. Death was life perverted. Hate was love perverted. Fear was faith perverted (pg. 5).”

In the Garden of Eden, after Adam and Eve sinned, the first words Adam spoke to God were, “I was afraid” (Genesis 3:10). The enemy is here to steal, kill, and destroy. So, he took the faith that Adam had, and it was turned to fear. I love where it’s explained, “The counterfeit never is as powerful as the real thing” (pg. 7). Therefore, we know that when we put faith to work, “it will always overcome fear.”

The Complexity of Anxiety and Fear

As I reflect on those years, I also recognize that fear and anxiety can be complex. While my journey involved learning to trust God more deeply and renew my mind with His Word, I realize that not everyone experiences fear in the same way.

Some people have lived through traumatic events, loss, abuse, or other painful experiences that leave their nervous system on high alert. Others struggle with anxiety disorders, panic attacks, obsessive thoughts, or other mental health concerns that involve biological, emotional, and environmental factors.

Practical Steps When Fear Feels Overwhelming

  • Identify the fearful thought.
  • Ask whether there is evidence of an actual present danger.
  • Compare that thought with God’s truth in Scripture.
  • Pray honestly about your fears.
  • Pray specific and related scriptures out loud (I will list some below).
  • Reach out to trusted believers or a counselor when fear becomes persistent or overwhelming.
  • Limit media that continually fuels fear.
  • Remember that courage often means moving forward while still feeling afraid.

For me, freedom came through prayer, Scripture, renewing my mind through books and other resources, and learning to trust God’s promises. For others, that journey may also include counseling, support groups, trauma work, medical care, or a combination of these resources. God can use all of these tools as part of His healing process.

But in our everyday Christian walk, we have to walk by faith. In doing so, we have to know the Word of God and stand on its principles. We have to know that Satan is under our feet because of what Jesus has done for us. As believers, we are free from every part of the curse.

So, why do we allow him to pull us around on strings of fear, worry, anxiety, depression, etc.? Yes, we are physical beings and will have physical problems, but God is bigger than any of our problems, and He has put other people – professionals – here on earth to help us walk through some of the pains of life.

Even though we know these truths, many of us still wrestle with fear, worry, anxiety, and discouragement. Sometimes these struggles are connected to painful experiences, ingrained thought patterns, or circumstances beyond our control. Yet God’s promises remain true. He meets us in our struggles and patiently helps us grow in faith as we learn to trust Him more fully.

For believers, Scripture is the foundation for confronting fear – both the fears rooted in reality and the ones shaped by our thoughts and emotions. God can also place different resources in our paths to help us confront fear and work through the layered process of renewing the mind. We can’t just stop at reading the Scripture; we have to believe it and apply it.

James 1:22 tells us, “But don’t just listen to God’s word. You must do what it says.” We have to speak the Word and believe what we are saying. When we speak His promises, we must remember the authority that we have through Jesus and speak it with confidence, not with hesitation.

As believers, we must take every thought captive (2 Cor. 10:5). Then, we must renew our minds with the Word of God (Rom. 12:2). I will share some of my favorite passages below. 365 references in the Bible say or address, “Do not fear.” Or as one of our friends says, “One ‘Do not fear’ for every day of the year!” (I love that!)

After I read Freedom from Fear, I knew that things were beginning to change in my thought life, but it wasn’t until a women’s retreat (my first retreat with my church) that I truly became free and broke off the chains of fear. I had gone to get away, enjoy myself, and, of course, for the great teaching I would receive, but I didn’t realize it would be life-changing.

I went away still battling fear, but returned home freed from the hurts, bitterness, worry, and the rest of the lies the enemy had been telling me at that time.

Fear once dictated many of my decisions, stole my peace, and kept me awake at night. Today, I still face circumstances that could make me fearful, but I no longer live under fear’s control. Freedom did not come overnight; it came through renewing my mind with God’s Word, learning to trust Him more deeply, and choosing faith one step at a time.

Anderson (2017) says, “Courage is not the absence of fear. Courage is choosing to live by faith and doing what is right in the face of perceived fear-objects. Behind every irrational fear is a lie, which must be identified. Ask the Lord to reveal to your mind the nature of your fears and the irrational lies that compel them” (2017, p. 28).

If fear has become a constant companion in your life, know that you are not alone. Whether through prayer, Scripture, counseling, supportive relationships, or a combination of these resources, healing is possible. The Lord is for you. And because He is for you, fear does not have to have the final word.

As I’ve shared, freedom from fear did not happen overnight for me. It was a process of learning to recognize fearful thoughts, replacing them with truth, and choosing – sometimes moment by moment – to trust God. Healing often works the same way. It may involve different resources that God provides. While the journey looks different for each person, we can take comfort in knowing that God walks with us through every step.

Bible Verses to Ponder

The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid? When evildoers came upon me to devour my flesh, my adversaries and my enemies, they stumbled and fell. Though a host encamp against me, my heart will not fear; Though war arises against me, in spite of this I shall be confident. – Psalm 27:1-3, NKJV

The LORD is for me; I will not fear; What can man do to me? – Psalm 118:6, NASB

Don’t be afraid of those who want to kill your body; they cannot touch your soul. Fear (reverence) only God, who can destroy both soul and body in hell. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. so do not fear; you are more valuable than many sparrows. – Matthew 10:28, 30-31, NLT

Since the children have flesh and blood, he too shared in their humanity so that by his death he might break the power of him who holds the power of death – that is, the devil –  and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death. – Hebrews 2:14-15, NIV

Seeking support is not a sign of weak faith. God often works through the wisdom, support, and resources He provides through others. Please give our reception team a call and schedule an appointment.

References: 
Anderson, N. T. (2017). The steps to freedom in Christ: A biblical guide to help you resolve personal and spiritual conflicts and become a fruitful disciple of Jesus. Bethany House Publishers
Kenneth Copeland. (1997). Freedom from fear. Kenneth Copeland Publications.

item.title: The Positive and Negative Impacts of a Friendship Breakup
item.description:
A friendship breakup can be one of the most devastating things you will ever go through, more intense even than a romantic breakup. A close friend provides a safe place and an emotional foundation to your life. They know more intimate details about you than even family members and have seen certain sides of you that even spouses have not.

Society only acknowledges how difficult it is to break up with a romantic partner. Until it happens to them, people will overlook the unique kind of heartbreak you feel during a friendship breakup.

Sometimes friendship breakups happen in slow motion, over a period of years. It doesn’t hurt any less, and it is hard to categorize the pain. It is like a dull ache in your heart, and you feel destabilized, anxious, and sad whenever you remember them and the connection you once shared.

This is a different kind of grief because at any point, you could reach out to them and try to bridge the gap. However, you intuitively know that the friendship will never be what it once was, and that it would be easier to move on without them than try to rekindle that connection.

However, sometimes a friendship breakup is for the best. It is possible, and occasionally necessary, to call a time-out on a friendship. We all have a capacity for how much we can take and how much we are willing to invest in someone else’s life. Certain friendships can draw too much from you, or limit you in ways you wouldn’t have imagined. Rather than ghosting them or growing to resent them, it is better to confront the situation and cut the cord.

A Unique Kind of Grief

When you get involved in a romantic relationship, in the back of your mind, there is always a possibility that it might not work out. You simply don’t do that with a friend, though. Every close friendship becomes a safe place where you can drop your guard and fully be yourself.

Close friends become an integral part of your life in a way that a romantic partner never could. These are things you might take for granted, but losing them in a friendship breakup is one of the worst shocks you will ever experience.

Unfortunately, society doesn’t recognize the legitimacy of a friendship breakup. As a result, there are few structures in place to support a person going through one. This adds to the grief. Ironically, the one person you would have shared the pain with before is the one causing you the pain now. Regardless of how long they were a part of your life, you will feel their absence intensely.

Legitimate Reasons for a Friendship Breakup

A friendship breakup is not always a personal thing, though. It’s not always about drama, bad behavior, or hurt feelings. It is perfectly reasonable to break up with a friend because you are hurt, drained, or affected by something they’re doing or failing to do.

People often hold onto unhealthy friendships out of a sense of loyalty or because they don’t know how to let them go. It’s easier to break up with a romantic partner because there are multiple examples of how to do that in every piece of media you consume. How and why does a person break up with a friend, though?

Moving in different directions

Both literal and figurative proximity matter in friendships. Some of the deepest connections with people are elastic, and they stretch across time, distance, and change. These friendships remain secure and important regardless of when you last saw each other or what path you’re currently on. They are rare connections, though. Many friendships fall away simply because you are on different timelines in life.

It’s not unusual for certain friendships to fade in relevance over time. It still hurts when you look back and remember how involved you were in each other’s lives, and what the friendship once meant to you. You might even still have deep affection for them.

If needed, you can let go of friendships like these so that you can both focus on the path ahead, especially when they go in different directions. You can keep your affection for each other as a memory without lingering resentment.

Changing values

Regardless of our ability to adapt to change, it is all around us constantly. Many people go through coming-of-age chapters like school, young adulthood, careers, marriage, children, and middle age. However, others don’t experience these moments in the same way or at the same time. Even when our lives sync with our friends, we might find ourselves holding different values from the ones we used to have.

People like to say “agree to disagree” regarding core values and principles, and this is a civil attitude to take. This attitude does not make for a solid foundation for a lasting friendship, however.

As much as it can feel like a rug-pull when a close friend changes their outlook or personal values, it is an ordinary part of life. Whether your values no longer align or if they are now in opposition with each other, you can’t expect to maintain a friendship with the same depth and intensity as before.

Lopsided involvement

A recent study showed that a casual friendship will develop naturally after having spent 70 hours together. A close friendship requires over 200 hours together. Some people connect because their energy matches or because they have similarities. However, like a garden, a friendship develops not just over time, but with effort and intention. Most plants die when they are not watered, fertilized, or kept in ideal conditions.

Some people put in minimal effort. They only speak when spoken to, never remember important details, and offer nothing of themselves unless asked. You might hang onto people like this because they are family members, or because you’ve known each other for decades.

When you evaluate the value of the connection, though, you realize that you are giving far more than they are. Perhaps the resources you are investing in this particular friendship could be better used elsewhere.

The Mature Way of Handling a Friendship Breakup

If given the choice of being confronted with the reasons a friendship isn’t working anymore or slowly being phased out of a friend’s life, many people would prefer the latter. It requires less work, but there are good reasons for being direct when going through a friendship breakup.

Firstly, it’s better to know the reason why someone is distancing themselves from you. Without that, you will draw your own conclusions, which could lead to feeling bitter, resentful, wounded, victimized, and even vengeful. It is better to clear up doubt than to be left with questions, regrets, and resentment.

Next, there might be something that you both need to confront, and having a frank conversation about it is the only way to do that. Not everyone thrives with direct communication, but it is an opportunity to grow, not only in being assertive but also in taking accountability. Perhaps you need to hear your friend’s side of the story about your own behavior. It’s uncomfortable but necessary for growth.

Lastly, it gives you a rare opportunity to find closure. Breakups are hard enough to deal with when you’ve seen it coming for some time. On the other hand, some breakups are so sudden that they leave you reeling. Many people believe that they are not obligated to end a friendship formally. When you are open and honest with your friend about wanting to move on from the relationship, it honors both of you and provides closure.

If you are going through a friendship breakup, you might benefit from counseling. Perhaps you need some help in confronting a friendship that is holding you back or hurting you. We can connect you with a counselor who will help. Please consult our online catalog or contact our reception team for more information.

Photo:
“Man Watching Sunset”, Courtesy of Tim Marshall, Unsplash.com, CC0 License; 

The post The Positive and Negative Impacts of a Friendship Breakup appeared first on Bothell Christian Counseling.
